How Sinch modernized its enterprise data warehouse from Snowflake to BigQuery to power AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them.
  • Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia.
  • Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s latest, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

It has been revealed that as the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them. A prime example is Sinch, one of the world’s leading cloud communications and customer engagement (CPaaS) companies, which processes billions of customer interactions, SMS routing events, voice calls, and transactional messages.

Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia. To eliminate data silos, curb monthly billing spikes, establish a single governed source of truth, and unlock the next generation of predictive AI capabilities, Sinch partnered with Google Cloud Professional Services to migrate its enterprise data warehouse to Google BigQuery.

Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s latest, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture.

Before it embarked on this modernization journey, Sinch faced several architectural and operational friction points:.

Cross-regional data sprawl: The company’s separate Snowflake instances in the EU, US, and Australia required intricate inter-region replication, which caused  multi-directional dependencies and complex cross-warehouse data management.

Resource spikes and commercial inefficiencies: Heavy monthly billing runs drove severe compute spikes in the US, even as other regions had underutilized capacity.

Recent findings suggest that high-volume scanning vs. dialect disparities: A single US email event table could generate up to 100 TB of daily scans. Meanwhile, mission-critical SQL relied on Snowflake-specific concurrency and table-swapping paradigms for concurrency validation, which lacked 1:1 equivalents in cloud-native SQL.

“Google Cloud's engineering expertise helped us overcome several technical challenges during our migration, particularly around optimising Spark partitioning and restructuring incremental data loads. This allowed us to identify more efficient approaches, improve performance and ensure we built a scalable, reliable solution for the future.”Dan Peters, senior manager, Data Delivery, Sinch.

To mitigate operational risk and prevent downtime for Sinch’s critical enterprise workloads (including ERP and NetSuite integrations), we initiated a phased migration framework:.

A use case pilot validation: The migration kicked off with a dedicated use case MVP that spanned 20 tables and 125 GB of refined data and automatically validated end-to-end data fidelity.

Layered strategy for coupled pipelines: Rather than attempting to cleanly slice interconnected business domains in the EU, the team adopted a layered approach —  migrating raw and base (bronze and silver) layers, establishing automated data ingestion, and stabilizing core entities before repointing consumption marts.

Orchestration consolidation: Sinch consolidated 36 independent ETL workflows into a single parameterized orchestrator by using Google Cloud Workflows, which streamlined CI/CD deployment logic, and reduced operational overhead.

It has been revealed that sinch transitioned its data ingestion pipelines to Dataproc Serverless (running Apache Spark 3.5), which directly pulled refined data into native BigQuery tables from S3 and Databricks Unity Catalog. And to overcome batch quota limits and resource exhaustion on billion-row datasets, Sitch optimized jobs by increasing Spark repartitioning factors to 50.

For its incremental pipelines, the team eliminated data duplication while minimizing query read costs by replacing slow, keyless merge statements with an optimized insert-and-overwrite windowing strategy.

In a recent development, in order to accelerate the translation of more than 1,200 dbt models across global projects, Sinch utilized Google Cloud BigQuery Migration Service alongside a set of custom AI translation skills. Here’s how:.

The team refactored Snowflake-specific table versioning and concurrency management paradigms into deterministic transaction blocks and view abstraction pointers. This ensured atomic updates and consistent data access.

Sinch leveraged specialized Google skills for other regional migration — specifically the dbt-sf-to-bq-translator skill powered by the underlying BigQuery Translation API — to automate the conversion of dbt models from Snowflake to BigQuery SQL syntax. This significantly reduced manual refactoring effort and error rates.

Concurrency checks that relied on row-level locking were redesigned into serialized batch validations.

Integer overflow risks in massive calculation tables were solved by adopting a tiered precision strategy (favoring NUMERIC over BIGNUMERIC), which cut storage costs and preserved absolute precision.

According to recent reports, “Migrating over a thousand complex dbt models and translating legacy SQL required a robust, automated approach. Google Cloud's guidance on query restructuring helped us streamline pipeline development and remove compilation blockers. The team shared best practices for migrating code from Snowflake to BigQuery, such as replacing Snowflake SWAP WITH and hybrid-table patterns with BigQuery time travel. They also helped us build workflows that copy data from Snowflake to BigQuery and run our dbt jobs along the way, which sped up our move to BigQuery.”Varun Gupta, Senior Data Engineer, Sinch.

By completing the migration, Sinch successfully transformed the operational bottleneck of its global data footprint into a driver of enterprise growth:.

High data churn; lengthy multi-hour batch runs.

Significantly faster query and pipeline processing speeds across billions of records.

Unpredictable month-end billing spikes.

Predictable capacity management with BigQuery reservations and slot autoscaling.

Segmented data warehouses requiring external pipelines.

Native BQML and Vertex AI decision intelligence platform.

With its core European warehouse workloads stabilized on BigQuery and data validation consistently outperforming legacy benchmarks, Sinch is now expanding this modern blueprint across its Australian (SMB) and US analytics. The SMB instance migration is already in progress and is utilizing Antigravity skills for the Snowflake to BigQuery translation.

By unifying data storage, operational governance, and serverless compute, Sinch has built a resilient platform that delivers real-time messaging reliability today while positioning the company to capture the full potential of enterprise AI tomorrow.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (219 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27149v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Predictive world models learn to forecast observations, but accurate short-term predictions do not necessarily produce physically coherent behavior over longer horizons. We investigate how incorporating physical structure can strengthen world models while retaining their underlying predictive objectives. Across token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems, we study conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics. In planetary motion, angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, while the benefits of temporal regularization depend on the accompanying physical objective and representation. In visual models, generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads produces more faithful trajectories and phase-space evolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of how physical structure participates in prediction: improvements in an auxiliary physical readout or a local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon behavior. Evaluations across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts further reveal where these benefits persist and where generalization remains limited. Our study supports physical structure as a practical means of improving predictive world models and provides a unified framework for understanding its effects on representations, learned transitions, and autonomous rollouts. The central lesson is that effective physical inductive biases should help models both represent physical regularities and use them to generate future states.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

According to recent reports, LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

According to recent reports, edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SBS, a provider of regulatory reporting software for financial institutions, has teamed up with professional services firm Deloitte to build a reporting solution that gives European banks a clearer line of sight from raw data to submitted figures.

It has been revealed that the collaboration is built on BIRD, the Banks’ Integrated Reporting Dictionary, and is designed to help lenders keep pace with shifting obligations such as IReF and SRB VDS. It also addresses the growing emphasis on data traceability and control set out under BCBS 239/PERDARR.

At the centre of the partnership is a planned BIRD-native product running on SBS’s existing technology.

Sources indicate that the tool is intended to show banks exactly how their underlying data is transformed into reported numbers, strengthening their oversight of data, workflows and regulatory submissions. Greater visibility should make reports simpler to justify and to audit.

Rather than requiring a wholesale overhaul, the solution can be rolled out step by step, allowing institutions to extend their current reporting set-up as regulatory demands intensify.

Each firm contributes distinct strengths. SBS supplies an established regulatory reporting platform alongside long experience working with financial institutions. Deloitte adds deep knowledge of BIRD and regulatory reporting, covering both reporting processes and operating models.

It has been revealed that reflecting BIRD’s principle of being developed “for and by banks”, the two companies blueprint to agree a joint roadmap with banks themselves. As the project advances, participating banks will decide priorities and influence how reporting rules are built into the product.

Deloitte partner regulatory reporting Peter Schaap remarked, “Consolidation in the regulatory reporting market makes meaningful choice more crucial for banks, particularly with significant changes such as IReF and SRB VDS on the horizon. Banks should have a say in how fresh reporting requirements are translated into practice and the flexibility to adopt changes in a way that fits their existing processes. SBS’s regulatory reporting software and experience with financial institutions make it a strong collaborator in bringing that choice to banks.”.

SBS CCOO Raouf Mhenni added, “Financial institutions across Europe trust SBS as a long-term partner, and that trust shapes how we work. Together with Deloitte, we want to give our clients a real say in the solutions they rely on, and a clearer view of the data and processes behind them. It is about delivering outcomes they can count on.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions, in both the Free Tier and Advanced Tier of VPC IPAM.

Industry observers note that amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) IP Address Manager (IPAM) policies now support AWS Network Firewall automated internet firewall and AWS Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs. You can centrally configure IPAM policies across AWS accounts and AWS Regions to allocate public IPv4 addresses to these resources from specific IPAM pools, such as Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP) addresses or Amazon-provided contiguous IPv4 blocks. This enables a stronger security posture, simplifies network and security operations, and can reduce public IPv4 costs when you use BYOIP.

Industry observers note that many customers allowlist the public IPs of their AWS resources in network access control lists (ACLs) and firewalls. Previously, keeping these resources on allowlisted addresses depended on each application team. With this launch, you can define allocation rules for them alongside existing resource types, so security teams can add IP-based filters with confidence that these resources draw addresses from approved ranges. For Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs, this covers the public IPv4 addresses used for outbound traffic through Lambda Network Connectors. If a pool runs out of addresses, resources fall back to Amazon-provided addresses. You can also share allocated ranges with partners through IPAM integration with AWS prefix lists.

The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions, in both the Free Tier and Advanced Tier of VPC IPAM. To learn more, see the IPAM policies documentation page and the IPAM documentation. For pricing details, see the IPAM tab on the Amazon VPC Pricing page.

Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (258 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27138v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.

According to recent reports, with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

Recent findings suggest that A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

Recent findings suggest that A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

According to recent reports, let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

Recent findings suggest that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

According to recent reports, every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

According to recent reports, each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

It has been revealed that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

In a recent development, text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps demonstrates how the image takes shape:.

In a recent development, the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

Breaking: Amazon Route 53 now supports Availability Zone (AZ) affinity routing

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (291 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Route 53 now supports Availability Zone (AZ) affinity routing, which routes DNS queries from your VPCs to resources in the same AZ as the client that sends the query.
  • Sources indicate that until now, customers who wanted lower latency used other routing policies, such as latency-based or geoproximity routing.
  • To get started, create AZ-affinity records and choose a location type for each: Availability Zone, Zone Group, Region, or Global.

Amazon Route 53 now supports Availability Zone (AZ) affinity routing, which routes DNS queries from your VPCs to resources in the same AZ as the client that sends the query. This helps you keep traffic within the same AZ as the client, reducing latency and improving application performance.

Sources indicate that until now, customers who wanted lower latency used other routing policies, such as latency-based or geoproximity routing. With this launch, DNS queries from your clients are answered with resources in the same AZ. This keeps traffic within the AZ and gives your clients faster responses. If there's no record for the client's AZ, Route 53 falls back to a record for a less specific location: the Zone Group, then the AWS Region, and then Global, in the same order.

To get started, create AZ-affinity records and choose a location type for each: Availability Zone, Zone Group, Region, or Global. For Availability Zone records, specify the AZ ID, such as use1-az1. You can associate a health check with any AZ-affinity record, whether it's for an AZ, a Zone Group, or a Region. If the endpoint is unhealthy, Route 53 answers with the record for the next location. You can use AZ-affinity routing for records in both public and private hosted zones. The Global record answers queries that don't come from your VPCs, such as queries from the internet. You can create AZ-affinity records with the Route 53 console, API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation.

AZ-affinity routing is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Route 53 public and private hosted zones are available. To learn more, see the AZ-affinity routing topic in the Route 53 Developer Guide. For pricing, see the Route 53 pricing page.

MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (137 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27133v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the fresh modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

Industry observers note that the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Sources indicate that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Industry observers note that muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

In a recent development, the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Industry observers note that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Industry observers note that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

In a recent development, video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

According to recent reports, the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

Sources indicate that <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:.

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:.

Sources indicate that the repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

It has been revealed that we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

According to recent reports, once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning indicates up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

In a recent development, the language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

According to recent reports, this is a significant model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/upcoming/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

Recent findings suggest that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section highlights how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

In a recent development, first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In a recent development, in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

Recent findings suggest that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

Recent findings suggest that we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

In a recent development, we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

It has been revealed that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27121v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.

Industry News: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.

Latest Update: Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

According to recent reports, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

According to recent reports, the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the upcoming release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

According to recent reports, we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Industry observers note that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Sources indicate that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

It has been revealed that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

In a recent development, if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (179 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies, giving you fine-grained control over which database objects are audited.
  • With object-level audit policies, you can focus on auditing the objects that matter most — for example, a single table that contains sensitive data or a specific user — without generating audit records for your entire database.
  • Sources indicate that amazon RDS provides stored procedures to create, modify, attach, detach, and drop object-level audit policies.

Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies, giving you fine-grained control over which database objects are audited. You can create custom audit policies and attach them to specific tables, users, groups, roles, and authorities in your RDS for Db2 databases.

With object-level audit policies, you can focus on auditing the objects that matter most — for example, a single table that contains sensitive data or a specific user — without generating audit records for your entire database. Object-level audit policies complement the existing database-level audit logging in Amazon RDS for Db2. You can use both at the same time, and they operate independently.

Sources indicate that amazon RDS provides stored procedures to create, modify, attach, detach, and drop object-level audit policies. Audit records are uploaded to the same Amazon S3 bucket that you configured for Db2 audit logging.

It has been revealed that object-level audit policies for Amazon RDS for Db2 are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is available. To get started see the Amazon RDS User Guide.

#26357. Breaking: Can AI investment give RegTech firms a lasting competitive edge?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1984 w)

Breaking: Can AI investment give RegTech firms a lasting competitive edge?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that regTech firms are investing heavily in AI, but the scale of that investment alone will not determine who comes out ahead.
  • Recent findings suggest that regTech Analyst and Parker & Lawrence Research recently published a major industry report examining the global state of RegTech in 2026.
  • FinTech Global recently sat down with several leading players in RegTech to get their thoughts on these findings in a second part of a two-part series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that regTech firms are investing heavily in AI, but the scale of that investment alone will not determine who comes out ahead. As AI capabilities become increasingly accessible, the competitive advantage will lie in how effectively firms translate them into better products, stronger customer outcomes and more differentiated offerings.

Recent findings suggest that regTech Analyst and Parker & Lawrence Research recently published a major industry report examining the global state of RegTech in 2026. As part of their findings, they looked at the return on investment on the commercial benefits of AI, and how this differed based on business size.

FinTech Global recently sat down with several leading players in RegTech to get their thoughts on these findings in a second part of a two-part series.

Why are some firms in the market generating significantly higher returns from AI than others?

In the view of Sarah French, CRO of TaxTec, the difference often comes down to whether organisations are investing in technology to solve a clearly defined business problem or simply investing in AI because they feel they should.

She remarked, “There is a significant difference between introducing automation and fundamentally improving how an operation functions.”.

It has been revealed that “For example, in financial services, many processes remain dependent on manual investigation, fragmented information, specialist knowledge and multiple operational touchpoints. Automating individual tasks may deliver incremental efficiencies, but the greater value comes from looking at the entire operating model and identifying where complexity can be removed.”.

For French, organisations that understand their operational challenges, establish clear objectives and measure outcomes are better positioned to realise meaningful returns from their technology investments.

Meanwhile, Areg Nzsdejan, CEO of Cardamon, remarked that the interesting thing for him in the survey was how little separates the groups of reduced manual effort.

According to recent reports, he remarked, “50.6% of the highest-ROI group report it, compared with 47.5% of the lowest. The gaps are much wider for faster onboarding, approvals or reviews, at 43.4% versus 27.5%, and faster product launches or market expansion, at 18.1% versus 2.5%.”.

These, he makes clear, are reported benefits, so the figures do not establish what caused the higher returns.

For the Cardamon CEO, however, they do suggest a useful question: has the time saved changed what the business can do?

“Automating a task creates limited commercial value if the same approval queue still holds everything up,” he stresses.

In the view of Anthony Quinn, CEO of Arctic Intelligence, the organisations who are seeing real returns from AI aren’t the ones automating the most tasks.

“They’re the ones who’ve tied AI to a specific customer outcome, such as faster, more defensible risk decisions, and built it into the product rather than bolting it on,” he explained.

In the view of Andrew Davies, global head of FCC strategy at ComplyAdvantage, the gap usually comes down to how the investment was scoped, rather than which model was selected.

He explained, “In our 2026 State of Financial Crime Report, 48% of compliance leaders reported that their firms have dedicated projects and budgets for AI in financial crime. Almost as many (46%) reported that their AI budget is confined to specific teams or siloed parts of the technology stack. Ultimately, an investment scoped to a single function returns value to only that function.”.

For Davies, there is a second, less comfortable explanation. Almost nine in ten respondents – 88% – admitted that including AI in a proposed compliance modernization program increases the likelihood of gaining approval and securing resources.

He remarked, “AI is simply easier to fund than most compliance technology, which means some programs are approved on the strength of the “AI” label rather than the viability of the business case. Firms that defined their desired outcomes first – such as fewer false positives, faster remediation, or better risk scoring – have something to measure returns against. Firms that funded the technology first simply do not.”.

How can RegTech firms move beyond automation to drive growth and commercial value?

In the opinion of Davies, buyers are already making that shift. He highlighted how when asked about the outcomes they have seen or expect from agentic and predictive AI, respondents named increased efficiency first at 54%, followed by improved customer experience and satisfaction at 51% – significantly ahead of cost reduction at 26%.

He commented, “The commercial case for AI in compliance is being built on driving growth rather than just savings: faster onboarding, fewer legitimate customers held in review, and less friction between a firm and its revenue.”.

For the FCC head, the real opportunity lies in the work that companies have not yet automated.

Davies stated, “Auto-remediation of level-one alerts is at the moment the least-implemented capability at 32%, behind suspicious activity detection at 55% and transaction monitoring at 53%. And while 95% of compliance leaders agree automation of routine work would be highly helpful, not a single respondent reported already having that capability – an unmet need in the highest-volume, lowest-judgment part of the workflow.”.

Meanwhile, for Nzsdejan, he suggested firms should start with a business decision that compliance work is delaying.

“For a latest product or market, a firm needs to establish which obligations apply, what it already covers and what has to change. At Cardamon, we speed up that assessment by mapping regulatory obligations against existing policies and controls, helping teams identify gaps and the work needed to close them earlier,” he said.

With this, firms can reduce compliance delays to a product launch or entry into a latest market, while keeping the same standard of review.

In a recent development, he added, “RegTech providers should measure the whole process. Time to an approved decision, rework and cost per completed assessment are more useful than the number of documents summarised.

Recent findings suggest that “For the provider, reusable workflows can also reduce implementation costs and make it economical to serve more customers. That advantage depends on how much specialist work is still needed for each deployment.”.

Quinn, however, is succinct, “Automation cuts cost, but it’s a race to the bottom. Commercial value comes from using AI to deliver insight customers couldn’t get before.”.

For French, the opportunity extends well beyond reducing processing time or operational costs.

“Technology can enable financial institutions to deliver services that would previously have been commercially difficult to provide, improve the experience for their clients and scale operations without a corresponding increase in resources,” she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that french mentioned that withholding tax recovery is a good example. “Historically, the operational effort involved in identifying, documenting, submitting and tracking reclaims has created barriers to delivering these services efficiently. Technology can help change that equation by centralising information, improving workflow management, reducing manual intervention and providing greater transparency over recovery opportunities.”.

In a recent development, the commercial value, she added, is not simply in doing the same work faster. It is enabling institutions to identify additional opportunities, improve service delivery and make previously resource-intensive activities commercially viable.

She went on, “AI may accelerate this further, but its value needs to be measured against tangible business outcomes rather than the sophistication of the technology itself.”.

What separates firms that successfully scale AI from those struggling to realise its potential?

The firms that struggle to scale tend to treat AI as a project, noted Quinn. The ones that succeed, he believes, treat it as an operating model, with clean data, clear governance and a roadmap tied to revenue.

On the other hand, French made clear her view that successful organisations recognise that technology adoption is as much an operational and strategic challenge as it is a technical one.

She said, “Scalability requires reliable data, clear processes, effective governance and integration with the wider technology environment.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, it also requires an understanding of where human expertise remains vital. For example, inhighly specialised areas such as tax and regulatory operations, technology should support experienced professionals by removing repetitive activities and improving access to information, rather than assuming every decision can or should be automated.

She commented, “The organisations that succeed will be those that combine technological capability with genuine subject-matter expertise and a clear understanding of their clients’ operating environments.

It has been revealed that “Ultimately, competitive advantage will not come from simply having AI. It will come from how effectively that technology translates into better outcomes for clients, stronger operational resilience and sustainable commercial growth.”.

Nszdejan believes that the scalers make it possible to repeat a good result.

According to recent reports, he explained, “A pilot can work because a few experts quietly correct the output. Scaling requires those corrections to become test cases, clear review rules and improvements to the underlying workflow.

“Teams need realistic examples of both routine and difficult work, and they need to test again when the model or source material changes. Someone must own the process and decide when an uncertain answer goes to a person.”.

Sources indicate that the economics for the Cardamon CEO should involve ongoing maintenance. If each new customer requires another layer of manual checking, the cost of delivery will keep rising with revenue, he stated.

Sources indicate that in the view of Davies, the bar has moved, and the regulator is helping set it. Speaking at the Bloomberg UK Policy Series on October 19, 2026, Jessica Rusu, the Financial Conduct Authority’s Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer, outlined the FCA’s vision for an “agentic regulator”.

Recent findings suggest that the watchdog is developing its own agentic tools to automate supervision, with initial deployments monitoring around 9,000 smaller wholesale firms filing transaction reports. It is also preparing to oversee the anti-money laundering controls of a further 60,000 firms expected to enter its remit from 2028.

According to Davies, the significance extends beyond the scale of these operations. As regulators themselves adopt AI to strengthen supervision, firms face growing pressure to demonstrate that they can monitor, explain and assure how their own systems behave in production.

Industry observers note that AI governance can no longer be treated as a periodic exercise. It must become a continuous function, embedded throughout the deployment lifecycle. This is increasingly the dividing line between firms scaling AI successfully and those struggling to move beyond pilots.

Sources indicate that however, for Davies, the biggest obstacle is often not the technology itself, but the architecture supporting it. Organisations operate an average of seven separate systems for each compliance activity, spanning customer screening, transaction monitoring, case management and regulatory reporting.

Deploying AI across this fragmented infrastructure risks reproducing the very data gaps, inconsistencies and operational blind spots that firms are trying to eliminate.

Adoption figures illustrate the gap between ambition and execution. For standard AI in customer screening, 93% of firms are using, piloting or evaluating a vendor solution, with 62% having successfully moved into production. Agentic AI presents a different picture. Although 73% are using, piloting or evaluating the technology, just 33% have reached production.

Davies believes that successful AI deployment depends on more than selecting the right model. Firms must first establish the data foundations, system connectivity and governance needed to support it. Increasingly, these are not simply prerequisites for scaling AI. They are also essential to keeping pace with a regulator that is becoming more technologically capable itself.

Davies concluded, “The firms seeing real returns from AI didn’t start with the model. They started by defining what a good outcome looks like, then ensuring they could measure it continuously.

Sources indicate that “This is no longer just good practice – when the regulator is running its own agentic tools, a system that cannot demonstrate how it behaves in production becomes a liability rather than an advantage. Almost every firm expects AI to deliver. Far fewer have built the data foundation that allows it to do so.”.

Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (193 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27100v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. Specifically, we represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two complementary axes: dependence explained by semantic support versus additional reasoning history, and dependence allocated to answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning. This decomposition yields global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency. Controlled interventions show that the proposed metrics respond to hidden dependence and induced off-path reasoning as intended. Across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks, answer-level unfaithfulness is consistently associated with greater predictive uncertainty, whereas both unfaithfulness and inefficiency exhibit weak or inconsistent associations with answer correctness. We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.
