Recent findings suggest that AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions in AWS Trusted Advisor. These recommendations identify on-demand functions where moving to Lambda Managed Instances (LMI) is estimated to reduce costs, and provide configuration guidance for running on LMI. With these recommendations, you can lower your Lambda costs by focusing your efforts on the functions with the greatest estimated savings.

According to recent reports, LMI lets you run Lambda functions on Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With LMI, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing options such as Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, without managing infrastructure. Previously, to determine whether a function was a good fit for LMI, you had to analyze its invocation patterns, estimate LMI costs, and select the right instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio yourself. This manual process added overhead and delayed savings. With this launch, Lambda automatically analyzes the invocation patterns, duration, and resource utilization of your high-volume Event Functions and recommends those where LMI is estimated to reduce costs. Estimates are based on a simulation of each function's invocation patterns, using public Lambda pricing and Amazon EC2 On-Demand pricing. Each recommendation includes the function ARN, the recommended EC2 instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio, the estimated current cost, the estimated LMI cost, and the estimated savings. You can use the recommended configuration to run a function on LMI without sizing it yourself and realize cost savings sooner.

These recommendations are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), and Europe (Milan). Customers with eligible AWS Support looks can access them in the Trusted Advisor console alongside other cost optimization checks. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide, the AWS Trusted Advisor User Guide, and the AWS Lambda pricing.

#26271. Breaking: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1716 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • According to recent reports, to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • It has been revealed that today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

According to recent reports, to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

It has been revealed that today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

Industry observers note that LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

It has been revealed that the LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

It has been revealed that the role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

According to recent reports, indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

It has been revealed that we compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

Recent findings suggest that all non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

According to recent reports, safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

In a recent development, LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

Recent findings suggest that LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

Latest Update: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.18531v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

Builders using the fresh AWS experience on the Paid strategy can now receive spend limit alerts by text message (SMS), alongside existing email notifications. A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost for a project. Notifications are sent as a project approaches its limit, and when a project reaches its limit, AWS automatically pauses it. SMS gives builders a second way to stay informed about their project costs.

Sources indicate that email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused. SMS alerts close this gap with a text message when a project's actual costs reach 90% of its spend limit, so builders have time to act, such as raising the limit or stopping resources they don't need.

In a recent development, to turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits. Text alerts are only sent to verified numbers, and you can opt out at any time. SMS alerts for spend limits are available at no additional charge for US phone numbers, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa.

To learn more, see Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, the AWS Account Management Reference Guide, or Get started with AWS.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

During the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly crucial in our everyday lives. Every upcoming integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:.

It has been revealed that we are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

Industry observers note that the project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

Sources indicate that to reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the at the moment implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. At the moment, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

In a recent development, the llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

arXiv:2611.14325v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.

arXiv:2611.23354v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

It has been revealed that you can now set cluster-wide include and exclude lists for namespaces, metric names, and pod and node labels. Because ingestion is billed per GB, collecting less lowers what you pay, and you can adjust filters with a single add-on configuration upgrade as your clusters change.

Telemetry sent through the add-on is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Industry observers note that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

It has been revealed that the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

Industry observers note that on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

Recent findings suggest that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million consumers, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the upcoming routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

It has been revealed that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

According to recent reports, routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics reveals the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

In a recent development, requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Tech Report: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (289 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.20242v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, compute futures are listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. The contracts on CME and ICE reference published short-dated rental rates, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.4%.

We forecast the realized volatility of 50 assets in equities, currencies and futures from the VOLARE dataset one, five and 22 days ahead, and compare the forecasts with pairwise and multi-model tests. The foundation models do not outperform the econometric benchmarks as a class. Only Tiny Time Mixers (TTM), the smallest of them, has a lower average QLIKE loss than the logarithmic HAR (Log-HAR) at every tested horizon, by a narrow margin. For most assets, the Model Confidence Set (MCS) contains TTM together with Log-HAR and several other models. Accuracy differs far more across the foundation models than between the best of them and Log-HAR, so which foundation model one chooses matters more than whether one uses a foundation model or an econometric one. For an investor who targets a constant volatility, TTM's edge is worth a few basis points a year before trading costs. Since TTM and Log-HAR make different errors, their equal-weight average matches the best single model and enters the MCS for nearly every asset.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Industry observers note that rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

It has been revealed that to find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

Recent findings suggest that on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

Industry observers note that on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

Sources indicate that the weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

Industry observers note that we're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

Latest Update: AWS Private CA now supports X.509 IAM condition keys

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (303 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued.
  • Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains.
  • You can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).

AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued. You can write IAM policies that allow or deny a certificate request based on its subject, subject alternative names (SANs), public key, signature algorithm, validity period, key usage, extended key usage, and basic constraints. You can share one private CA across teams and accounts, and each team can issue only the certificates your policies allow.

Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains. To keep each team to its own domain names, customers ran a separate CA for each team or built their own authorization layer in front of AWS Private CA. Now, AWS Private CA evaluates your policies against the certificate as it would be issued, before anything is signed, and denies requests that don't comply. For example, you can limit each account to DNS names in its own subdomain, cap certificate lifetimes, require specified key algorithms and key sizes across your organization, and reserve CA certificates for your PKI team.

You can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Each key takes its value from the final certificate, whether the attribute comes from the certificate signing request (CSR), the certificate template, or API passthrough, so moving an attribute to a different input doesn't get it past a policy.

Industry observers note that X.509 IAM condition keys are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where AWS Private CA is available. AWS Private CA charges still apply. To get started, see X.509 certificate condition keys in the AWS Private CA User Guide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • Sources indicate that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
  • In a recent development, orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

Sources indicate that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

In a recent development, orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

In a recent development, my first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

According to recent reports, that's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Recent findings suggest that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's massive batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Sources indicate that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

Recent findings suggest that if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the significant model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

It has been revealed that all of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

Recent findings suggest that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

Sources indicate that I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Sources indicate that experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

Sources indicate that the API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization initiative of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

Sources indicate that the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

Industry observers note that the model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Industry observers note that strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Sources indicate that most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

In a recent development, most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

Sources indicate that it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Recent findings suggest that beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

Industry observers note that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Industry observers note that finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2505.14548v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We offer evidence that federal emergency assistance (FEMA) in the days following natural disasters mitigate evictions in comparison to similar emergency scenarios where FEMA aid is not provided. We find an approximate 10.9% increase in overall evictions after hurricane natural disaster events driven in large part by areas in close proximity of the hurricane path that do not receive FEMA rental assistance. Furthermore, we also show that FEMA aid acts as a liquidity buffer to other forms of emergency credit, specifically we find that overall transactions volumes decrease during hurricane events in locations that do receive FEMA aid. This effect largely reverses in areas that do not receive FEMA aid. Overall, this suggests that the availability of emergency liquidity during natural disaster events is indeed a binding constraint with real household financial consequences, in particular through our documented channel of evictions and in usage of high-cost credit.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that amazon Transcribe now offers a synchronous transcription API, TranscribeAudio. Send a complete audio file in a single request and get the full transcript back in the same response. There is no job to start, no status to poll, no connection to manage. The transcripts are as accurate as Amazon Transcribe batch transcription, so you can add fast, accurate speech-to-text to interactive applications such as voice assistants, agent-assist tools and on-demand "transcribe this clip" features.

The synchronous API supports the Amazon Transcribe features you already use, including:.

Sources indicate that send audio inline (up to 25 MB) or from Amazon S3 (up to 500 MB), 0.5 seconds to 1 hour long, in WAV, MP3, FLAC, M4A, MP4, Ogg, WebM or AMR format. The transcript comes back in the response, or Transcribe can write it to an S3 location you choose. Pricing is $0.0070 per minute of audio, billed per second, with speaker diarization, language identification, custom vocabulary and channel identification included. Two-channel audio is billed once on file duration. PII redaction is available as an add-on.

Recent findings suggest that supports English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Korean and Chinese (Simplified, Traditional and Hong Kong). Available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Ireland, London, Frankfurt), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul) and South America (São Paulo), with PII redaction available in all stated Regions except South America (São Paulo).

To get started, see Amazon Transcribe API Reference and the Amazon Transcribe pricing page.

Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack.

You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey. You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (282 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.26948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before consumers incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $\Theta(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.
